name: Pralayakaleswarar Temple, Pennadam (Thoongaanai Maadam)
deity: Shiva as Sudarkozhundeesar (Pralayakaleswarar), with the Goddess Kadanthai Nayaki (Amudhanayaki)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu, the Kadanthai of the Tevaram, sung by Appar and Sambandar (7th century)
dynasty: Chola country of the Vellar valley, with later additions
summary: At Pennadam, the Tevaram's Kadanthai, Shiva saved the town from the deluge: his elephant-backed shrine, Thoongaanai Maadam, is where Appar was marked with the trident and the bull.

sections.history: Pennadam is a town in Cuddalore district, about 18 km south-west of Virudhachalam on the road to Tittagudi. The Tevaram calls the town Kadanthai and its Shiva temple Thoongaanai Maadam, the shrine shaped like a sleeping elephant. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and is counted second among those of Nadu Nadu; both Appar and Thirugnana Sambandar sang a pathigam here. The town also has its own place among the sixty-three Nayanmars as the home of Kalikamba Nayanar, whose life the Periya Puranam tells, and pilgrims often go on from here to Arathurai, a few kilometres to the south-west.
sections.architecture: The shrine takes its Tevaram name from its form: the sanctum roof is gajaprishta, curved like the back of an elephant, a rarer vimana type among the Tamil temples. Within it the Lord is worshipped as Sudarkozhundeesar, the radiant flame, while the Goddess, Kadanthai Nayaki, has her own shrine. Unusually, the Nandi here faces away from the sanctum, towards the town, and the reason for his turned gaze is the temple's great legend.
sections.legends: Tradition tells that when the waters of the pralaya, the great deluge, rose to engulf the place, Shiva commanded Nandi to turn around and drink the flood, and the temple and its people were saved; so the Lord is Pralayakaleswarar and his bull still stands guard facing outward. Here too, it is said, Appar, returning to Shaivism, prayed to bear the Lord's marks, and was blessed with the emblems of the trident and the bull upon his shoulders.
sections.festivals: Pradosham is kept with particular devotion before the turned Nandi, alongside Maha Shivaratri, Arudra Darshanam and the festivals of the Goddess, Kadanthai Nayaki. Devotees of Appar also come to remember the saint's consecration at this shrine with special reverence; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Pennadam rewards an unhurried visit: walk around the sanctum to see the curve of its elephant-backed roof, then stand with the Nandi who faces the town and recall the deluge legend. For devotees of Appar it is a place of consecration, where the saint asked to be marked for ever as the Lord's own.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Pennadam lies about 18 km south-west of Virudhachalam on the Virudhachalam–Tittagudi road, with regular buses. Virudhachalam is the nearest major railway junction; Tiruchirappalli and Chennai are the nearest large airports.
